en: Kumaiyk in that enclosure
Let me drive out upon the road.
My orphan and Kanykei—
Let me find Kanykei.
I have searched the wilds so often.
At the place where he performed ablution,
Encountered through the unseen,
Found through God's favor,
Before its eyes had opened,
He gave it milk from his mouth,
Gave it meat with his hand,
Had a steel collar fitted to its neck,
Had a tiger-skin covering laid upon its back.
'A raiding hero needs it,' he said,
And had the tiger woman Kanykei rear it.
It never drew back from a tiger;
Like a bear, it never turned away.
Whatever it bit, it ravaged;
Everyone who saw it, it made smile.
When dear Manas died,
It laid its head upon the ground.
At the khan's burial enclosure then,
Kumaiyk lay down howling.
Khan Manas's little enclosure—
Kumaiyk in that enclosure
Let me drive out upon the road.
My orphan and Kanykei—
Let me find Kanykei.
I have searched the wilds so often.
Seeking what is lost in the unseen,
What desire could I fulfill?
Rather than that, from this world,
My precious Kumaiyk,
Let me depart while driving you onward.'
At the spur where the mountain ended,
At the level mountain's promontory,
Khan Manas's little enclosure—
Galloping toward that enclosure,
The leopard Bakai went.
Shouting toward the enclosure,
Calling out for Kumaiyk:
'My cherished Kumaiyk,
My wings have been broken back.
The one I took as my companion,
Semetey, I have lost!
O Kumaiyk, Kumaiyk!
I have no strength to gird myself;
The child the warrior left me is gone!
I have no strength to remain alive;
I have no garden planted in Talas.
The ruler of the multitude,
My child Kanykei is gone as well.
I have no foal tether stretched in Talas;
My pure, venerable mother is gone.
I have no garden planted in Keng-Kol.
Parted from the orphan without seeing him,
The hero Bakai has no good fortune.
His plucked-out beard had gathered in a heap;
Your falcon Khan Bakai stood in anguish.
Know, Kumaiyk, I tell you, know!
Know, and follow the trail, I tell you!
Be sure to lower your head to the ground.
My cherished Kumaiyk,
Be sure to find my orphan.
If you do not find my orphan,
If you cannot recognize his trail,
If you do not find my orphan,
Around the world's four corners,
If I do not chase you four times round,
If, driving you before me,
I do not force you into some pit,
May I never have been born;
May I die unworthy of the name Bakai!
Know, Kumaiyk, I tell you, know!
Know, and follow the trail, I tell you!
Kumaiyk, find him for me, I tell you.
Kumaiyk, if you do not find him,
To the earth's far end, Zhelpinish,
If I do not drive and chase you to Zhelpinish,
May I die unworthy of the name Bakai!
Find him, Kumaiyk; let me see him.
Know, Kumaiyk, I tell you, know!
Know, and follow the trail, I tell you!'
Roaring in anger,
He called out for Kumaiyk.
Inside the white mausoleum,
Kumaiyk stood howling.
Though an animal, it was bewildered;
Kumaiyk stood in misery.
Whimpering, its head to the earth
Kumaiyk lowered.
It had no tongue to speak with;
To what Bakai was saying,
Kumaiyk listened.
That accursed Kumaiyk
Bounded down into the lowlands,
Crept along the ridges.
The rolling, mottled northern slope
It sniffed along the forward trail.
The foothills along the bank-side road
It sniffed seven times.
Keng-Chapchak's broad ridge,
Kerme, the foot of Keng-Kol,
The slope of Üyrülmö
It sniffed three times.
Behind it Khan Bakai,
Making it stumble in haste,
Pressing it till its tail tucked down,
His bellow splitting stones,
Dear leopard Bakai,
His shout splitting heads,
Calling out for Kumaiyk,
Striking now and again,
Mighty Bakai drove it onward.
Out of its wits and stumbling,
Kumaiyk hurried on.
Whipped now and again,
Kumaiyk fled.
'If I do not make a spectacle for the ages,
You damned Kumaiyk,
If you do not find Kanykei for me,
If I do not cut off your head!'
His fiery eyes, unlike any others,
Blazed as Khan Bakai went.
Roaring and beating the hound,
Khan Bakai drove it onward.
Around Bel-Döbö of Üch-Kaikang
He chased it three times.
At its wits' end, the white hound
To Kaiypchy's Black Cave
Fled and stood there.
Khan Bakai's gray winged steed
Had lowered its head toward the earth.
The wind could not match its trot;
No animal could match its steps.
That day the gray winged steed
Had warmed to its running
And lowered its head toward the earth.
Unable to regain its composure,
To Kaiypchy's cave
It fled and stood there.
Of that brown wether taken there,
It found the bones.
The winding path she had walked crying out—
Kumaiyk examined it closely
And found the road she had taken.
When it saw Kanykei's trail,
Unable to restrain itself, Kumaiyk
Lowered its head to the ground.
Sniffing the black earth once,
It howled and howled,
Then set off at a run.
The lion Bakai, the leopard,
Behind the hound,
Whipping every which way,
Spurring from either side,
Without looking round about,
When the hound fled onward,
Bakai, the true holy man,
Did not spare his life at all.
Without scanning all around,
When the hound fled onward,
Holy Bakai, blessed by Khizyr,
Spared his life not even a hair's worth.
The dear lion, cocklike in bearing,
Raised a commotion, shouting.
That he would not cease pursuing,
When the hound realized this,
The white hound, wiser than a human,
Flattened its ears and lowered its head.
Sparing its wretched life no mercy,
When it came to a downward slope,
That accursed white hound
Sped far ahead like a shimmering haze.
When it began to climb,
Khan Bakai pressed close upon its heels.
When it entered a steep descent,
That accursed white hound,
Its flintlike eyes glittering—
As they pressed uphill,
Khan Bakai's gray winged steed,
Its bull-like neck swelling,
Chased after the white hound,
With Bakai, the two together.
Let us leave them thus.
Kanykei, who had departed in mourning,
Semetey, who had fled away—
Let us begin the tale of the widow.
Her breast filled with many sorrows,
Your fierce-wolf sister-in-law Kanykei,
Then her tears flowed ten ways.
'My river, vast as a lake when I look,
My cherished elder,
When I see you, my heart is content.
Mother, I have no refuge but you.
My consolation before me,
My mother whom I take as shelter,
My true refuge before me.
My bannered spear, my steadfast support,
Parted from your accomplished son,
Our happiness remained in Talas.
My cherished, sacred mother,
We did not die on the road in flight,
Nor, mother whom I cherish,
Die on a pass with no one in sight.
Rather than flee, beset by misfortune,
Mother, whom I cherish,
We did not die among the honored Kyrgyz people.
Mother whom I take as companion,
Has our strength failed us now?
Your only one whom we cradled
Has gone hungry for six days.
Mother, whom I cherish,
Has his death arrived today?
Your only one left by generous Manas—
His nose has grown pinched.
Will he go toward Judgment?
Mother, whom I cherish,
Dividing our grief-stricken hair into five,
Let us braid it close upon our heads.
For the only one my lord left behind,
Rather than remain alive, here in this place,
Let us die as his sacrifice.
If we remain alive instead,
And stagger on to Bukhara,
What wish will we fulfill?
Losing the heir my khan left behind
Here along the way,
Mother, how can we go on alive?
O my beloved mother,
Give me my Aktinte dagger; I will take it,
For the orphan granted after such suffering,
Let wretched me become a sacrifice!
My beloved mother,
That precious bird, the crane,
Stretches its flight across the plain, they say.
With this great head still on my shoulders,
I walked away from Talas,
Saying, ‘He is the child my khan left behind.’
God has granted us no way onward;
My beloved mother,
Will he be left in some ravine?
It seems his strength, too, is departing,
This child the Magnanimous One left behind.
My beloved mother,
I have no strength to give him my breast;
Not a scrap of strength remains in me.
We frantic women, crying out,
Have turned aside into this valley.
Mother, was this the day we were to die?
The child that noble man left behind—
Bereft of my only one,
My beloved mother,
From going out in search of food,
Dark blood has streamed from the soles of my feet.
This narrow world has closed upon me;
